summary.text: Seawater is the water of seas and oceans, and each kilogram of it carries about 35 grams of dissolved salts, mostly sodium and chloride.
Those salts make it denser than fresh water and lower its freezing point, so at typical saltiness it stays liquid down to about −2 °C.
Its surface pH was around 8.2 before 1850 and has been falling since, through a human-caused process called ocean acidification tied to carbon dioxide emissions.

items.prompt: On a very cold night, a bowl of seawater and a bowl of plain water sit side by side. Why does the seawater stay liquid longer as it cools?

options.label: Seawater stores more heat from the daytime sun
Its dissolved salt lowers the temperature at which it freezes
Salt crystals keep the water constantly moving
Seawater is lighter, so cold air passes over it

items.explain: The more salt is dissolved, the lower the freezing point; typical seawater freezes at about −2 °C.

items.prompt: A swimmer notices she floats more easily in the sea than in a pool of pure water. What best explains this?

options.label: Sea water is warmer, which pushes bodies upward
Waves constantly lift her toward the surface
Salts add more mass than volume, making the water denser
Salt soaks into her skin and makes her lighter

items.explain: Dissolved salts raise the water's mass by a larger proportion than its volume, so seawater is denser than pure water and gives more lift.

items.prompt: Roughly how much dissolved salt is in a one-litre bottle of typical seawater?

options.label: About 3.5 grams
About 150 grams
About 350 grams
About 35 grams

items.explain: Average seawater is about 3.5% salt, which works out to roughly 35 grams in each kilogram, about a litre.

items.prompt: A sea in a hot, dry region gets little rain, few rivers flow into it, and its water barely circulates with the open ocean. What would you expect of its water?

options.label: Saltier than typical seawater
Fresher than typical seawater
About average, as the ocean evens it out
Salty in summer but fresh every winter

items.explain: High evaporation, low rain, little river input and confined circulation make the Red Sea the saltiest open sea.

items.prompt: A research boat samples water beside a melting glacier and far out in the open ocean. What will it likely find near the glacier?

options.label: Saltier water, because ice pushes salt out
Less salty water, because meltwater mixes in
The same saltiness as everywhere else
Denser water, because it is so cold

items.explain: Where fresh water from glaciers, rivers or heavy rain mixes in, seawater can be much less saline.

items.prompt: In the 1990s, researchers began identifying sea microbes by probing short snippets of their DNA. What did that reveal?

options.label: Fewer kinds than lab cultures had suggested
That nearly all sea microbes were already known
Far more kinds of microbes than anyone expected
That deep seawater holds no living microbes

items.explain: The DNA methods turned up thousands of unknown microbes and showed a litre of seawater may hold over 20,000 species.

beats.title: The Salt That Changes Everything
beats.hook: Every kilogram of seawater hides about 35 grams of salt, and that salt changes how the water weighs, freezes and varies around the globe.

beats.prompt: You keep dissolving more salt into a jar of seawater. What happens to the temperature at which it will freeze?
beats.explain: Seawater's freezing point falls as its salt concentration rises; at typical salinity it freezes at about −2 °C.

choices.label: It rises, so it freezes sooner
choices.feedback: Salt feels like it should make water 'thicker' and quicker to set, but it works the other way.

choices.label: It stays the same; only temperature matters
choices.feedback: Freezing point depends on what is dissolved in the water, not just on how cold it gets.

choices.label: It drops, so it must get colder to freeze

beats.prompt: Sort each place by how its water compares with typical seawater.
beats.explain: Evaporation and confinement concentrate salt, while fresh water from rivers, ice melt and rain dilutes it.

beats.prompt: Match each property of seawater to its typical value.
beats.explain: These are the average figures for seawater; real values shift with place, temperature and time.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?

steps.text: Dissolving salt adds mass to water.
It adds proportionally less volume than mass.
So a litre of seawater has more mass than a litre of pure water.
So seawater is less dense than pure water.

beats.explain: More mass in the same volume means higher density: seawater is denser than both fresh and pure water.

beats.idea: Dissolved salts make seawater denser and slower to freeze than fresh water, and how much salt it holds varies from place to place.
